paragraphs: Caution signals | 25-1112.00 teaches law courses, including primarily teaching roles and roles combining teaching and research; deliverables include course materials, grading rationale, student guidance and research outputs. U.S. 2025 median annual pay is USD 128,500, with 10th/90th percentiles of 64,250/287,900. The newer BLS series for exact occupation 25-1112 projects employment from 25,800 in 2025 → 26,500 in 2035, growth of 2.6%, a table-listed net increase of 700 and 1,800 average annual openings, including growth and replacement, not net new jobs or current hiring. Handle academic concerns through institutional procedures; classroom status grants no lawyer authority. Nationwide Chinese pay gaps and industry references are listed separately.

Judgment required | Actual fit depends on doing three things in the same job: carrying out substantive teaching and research (designing courses around educational objectives, organizing classroom discussion, grading assignments and exams against clear standards, supervising theses and producing reviewable research); managing academic standards and student boundaries (grading standards and academic integrity, citation and data practices, student privacy and grade confidentiality, and distinguishing teaching discussion from legal advice on specific cases, under university policies and academic standards); and taking defined job responsibilities (for one's teaching content, grading rationale and research outputs, reporting academic misconduct concerns or matters outside teaching duties through procedures). Test this through a verifiable experience—using an entirely fictional syllabus to design one lesson, an assignment rubric and two sample grading decisions—rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Experience suggestion | Use the pathway LT-01's sole fictional R1 and two answers to produce a 10-minute lesson design, four-criterion grading, two feedback notes and a revision record. Verify A4/B0 aligns with lesson objectives; use no real students, exam questions, cases or generated legal provisions. Seven-day plan, 20—30 minutes daily: D1: copy exercise ID R1, Alpha/Beta and boundaries; D2: check objectives and 2+3+3+2=10 minutes; D3: write four grading criteria; D4: independently assign A4/B0 with rationale; D5: write two feedback notes and draft revisions; D6: ask a colleague to grade the same exercise and compare differences; D7: assemble four work samples and employer requirements pending verification. Paper simulation does not prove real teaching performance or teaching/lawyer authorization.

Fit signals | O*NET 25-1112.00 work activities focus on training and teaching others, creative thinking, interpreting and analyzing information, and communicating with peers and students. If you will repeatedly check alignment of teaching objectives and assessment, explain grading rationale clearly, sustain research and accept peer review, these everyday demands may align more closely with your working style. Interest and personality tools only help design trials, not judge teaching qualifications or performance.

Postsecondary law teachers 25-1112.00 teach law courses, including primarily teaching roles and combined teaching/research roles. O*NET tasks include classroom discussions, syllabus preparation, assessment and grading, research and publication, knowledge updates, student records and guidance, committee and administrative service, and some professional consultation. Teachers may separately hold lawful practitioner status, but teaching status itself grants no representation or legal-service authority. The newer BLS series for exact occupation 25-1112 projects employment from 25,800 in 2025 → 26,500 in 2035, growth of 2.6%, a table-listed net increase of 700 and 1,800 average annual openings, including growth and replacement, not net new jobs or current hiring. The older O*NET series shows employment of 29,500 in 2024 → 30,200 in 2034, growth of 2% and 2,200 average annual openings; keep newer and older series separate, without addition.

entries: Work objects | Conduct teaching and research on educational objectives and syllabi, legal textbooks and case materials, student assignments and theses, and research and academic exchange, within academic standards and university policies.

Results must be traceable to educational objectives and academic evidence.

Complete workflow | Define educational objectives and teaching hours → prepare syllabi and teaching materials → teach and facilitate discussion → prepare and grade assessments and provide feedback → guide students and conduct research → participate in academic service and keep content current.

This job first checks: objects (educational objectives and syllabi, textbooks and case materials, student assignments and theses, research questions); inputs (education plans and course standards, academic and citation requirements, grading and confidentiality rules); and deliverables (syllabi and teaching materials, rubrics and grading rationale, guidance and thesis feedback records, research outputs). Treat anything unverified as pending verification; experience or intuition cannot replace academic standards and evaluation evidence. This page does not constitute legal advice.

Assess the work loop in four steps: verify inputs (confirm educational objectives, academic standards and confidentiality requirements) → define tasks (work within teaching and research duties, without treating classroom discussion as legal advice on a specific case) → execute and record (complete teaching, grading and research with records) → review and escalate (stop immediately and report grading disputes, academic misconduct concerns and consultations beyond duties through procedures). A complete loop requires verifiable assessment and rationale, not simply finishing the course.

Which interests, abilities and working styles matter more for postsecondary law teachers? This page discusses fit through work samples and responsibility boundaries, without substituting personality labels for teaching qualifications or performance assessment.

Direct answer | Fit signals include willingness to repeatedly check and correct course design, grading and records, ability to explain grading rationale clearly, sustained research and acceptance of peer review, and procedural handling of grading disputes or consultations beyond duties. Personality labels or single test scores are not the basis. Interest and personality tools only help design trials, not judge teaching qualifications or performance.

Positive signals | You can design and align courses and assessments with educational objectives, grade using clear standards with reviewable feedback, and keep legal and case content current with proper citations.

Caution conditions | Risk signals include mismatched objectives and assessment, vague grading criteria causing disputes, improper citation or data practices, turning classroom discussion into conclusions on specific real cases, and leaks of student information or exam questions. If sustained research-output pressure and high competition are difficult to tolerate, weigh these as real costs.

Trial activity | Complete pathway LT-01 using only fictional R1, Alpha/Beta cases and A/B answers; verify A4/B0 and alignment of the 10-minute objective, delivering four work samples and a seven-day review. Use no real students, grades or cases.

Conclusion | Activity preferences align more closely with Social and Investigative interests (O*NET interest code SI, including teaching and education, social sciences and professional consultation). Interest codes only help design trials, not judge teaching qualifications or performance.

Assessment boundaries | This round did not establish predictive validity of personality scales for performance in this occupation. Continue checking with LT-01's four work samples and evidence of real authorized teaching and research; labels cannot establish hiring or qualifications.

Conclusion | RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help formulate questions. They cannot replace teaching qualifications, practice licenses, academic standards or evidence of actual teaching and research performance. No tool conclusion constitutes a hiring, qualification or authorization judgment.

Grading and academic integrity risks | Triggers: unclear rubrics, unsupported grade changes or improper handling of academic misconduct. Consequences: grade disputes and damage to academic trust. Controls: publish grading criteria and rationale, retain grading and review records, and handle academic misconduct concerns through university procedures. Boundary: academic integrity and grading systems follow university rules.

Research standards risks | Preserve originals and versions when citations, data or authorship are questionable, and report through university procedures. China's Ministry of Education Order No. 40 requires academic-integrity guidance and review and retention of original data; investigations and findings follow university and academic-committee procedures. A lead is not a personal finding of misconduct, and grading disputes are not automatically research misconduct.

Teaching and practice boundaries | Verify classroom discussion, course examples and commissioned legal services separately. Neither teacher status nor a disclaimer automatically authorizes lawyer representation. Chinese legal education and research personnel may apply lawfully for part-time practice; verify licensing and actual business permissions separately. For real-case inquiries, first define duties and refer onward; without verified authorization, do not act as a lawyer.

Student information and exam-question risks | All public teaching samples are fictional. Process real grades and unpublished exam questions only within university-approved permissions and environments; do not upload them to external generative tools. O*NET lists student-record duties; verify specific data-protection and examination systems under applicable institutional rules. This is work-practice guidance, not a fully verified set of regulations.

Workload and competition risks | Triggers: overlapping teaching, supervision and academic service, with sustained research-output and review pressure. Consequences: potential harm to teaching quality and personal health. Controls: prioritize teaching and research, retain essential preparation and assessment steps, and seek support and adjustments through procedures when needed. Boundary: workload and assessment arrangements follow institutional policy.

Fixed paper exercise LT-01: a fictional 10-minute lesson aims to distinguish conditions from exceptions in the original rule. The sole fictional rule R1: 'Complete materials may enter review; missing pages must be supplied before review; entering review does not mean approval.' Fictional case Alpha has complete materials but has not been reviewed; Beta lacks page 2. The assignment asks for each next step and a citation to R1. Each answer is out of 4: Alpha enters review, 1 point; Beta supplies the missing page first, 1 point; explaining review is not approval, 1 point; explicit R1 citation, 1 point. No corresponding content means no point. Fictional answer A: 'Alpha may enter review; Beta must supply page 2 first; review is not approval (R1)'; B: 'Alpha is approved; Beta goes directly to review; rule as above.' The draft awards both 4 and calls R1 real law. Deliver a 10-minute lesson design, criterion-by-criterion grading table, two feedback notes and a revision record. Use no real laws, cases, students or grades.

Reference deliverables: A=1+1+1+1=4, B=0+0+0+0=0; the original two scores of 4 are wrong. B's 'rule as above' lacks an explicit R1 citation. Alpha may only enter review, not claim approval; Beta must supply the missing page before review. R1 is a fictional rule, not a legal provision. Lesson design: 2 minutes reading R1, 3 comparing Alpha/Beta, 3 independently grading, 2 checking, totaling 10 minutes. Feedback cites R1 and the rubric item by item; incorrect grading does not establish real academic misconduct. The four work samples—lesson design/grading table/two feedback notes/revision record—demonstrate paper checks only.

Seven-day plan, 20—30 minutes daily: D1: copy exercise ID R1, Alpha/Beta and boundaries; D2: check objectives and 2+3+3+2=10 minutes; D3: write four grading criteria; D4: independently assign A4/B0 with rationale; D5: write two feedback notes and draft revisions; D6: ask a colleague to grade the same exercise and compare differences; D7: assemble four work samples and employer requirements pending verification. Paper simulation does not prove real teaching performance or teaching/lawyer authorization.

risks.consequence: May cause grade disputes and damage academic trust.
risks.mitigation: Publish grading criteria and rationale, retain grading and review records, and handle academic misconduct concerns through university procedures.
risks.scenario: Unclear rubrics, unsupported grade changes or improper handling of academic misconduct.

risks.consequence: May constitute academic misconduct and harm academic reputation.
risks.mitigation: Verify original citations, data and authorship, retain concerns and report through university procedures; do not determine findings yourself.
risks.scenario: Improper citation, questionable data or authorship disputes.

risks.consequence: May mislead students and exceed teaching and practice boundaries.
risks.mitigation: Verify identity and permissions separately for teaching and separately commissioned practice; refer onward before acting without verified authorization.
risks.scenario: Turning classroom discussion into legal conclusions on specific cases, or providing students legal advice beyond duties.

risks.consequence: May infringe student rights and affect assessment fairness.
risks.mitigation: Use only institution-approved environments for real grades and exam questions; all public samples are fictional.
risks.scenario: Unauthorized processing or disclosure of grades, student information or exam content.

risks.consequence: May affect teaching quality and personal health.
risks.mitigation: Prioritize teaching and research, retain essential preparation and assessment steps, and seek support and adjustments through procedures when needed.
risks.scenario: Overlapping teaching, supervision and academic service, with sustained research-output and review pressure.

risks.consequence: May cause procedural errors and boundary violations.
risks.mitigation: Stop related actions first, then report or refer facts, impacts and pending questions to authorized departments under university policy.
risks.scenario: Continuing to handle grading disputes, academic misconduct concerns or consultations beyond duties independently.
